notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0121g.stoa002.opp-l: 1.2.1: 'extra catholicam exui salutis' is evidently corrupt; 'exui' may stand for something like 'arca' (ark) or 'domo'; rendered tentatively as '[ark?] of salvation'. 1.1.1: the Greek numerals are T (300, the cross) and IH (18, the opening of the name Jesus). 1.1.2: 'cuilibet ... homini' and the contrast with 'in illum' rests on credere + dative versus credere in + accusative. 1.2.2: stray 'ab)' read as a footnote mark. 1.4 heading: 'ADSERBNDA' read as 'adserenda'. Line 21: the scan's 'exui' is read as exul.

Scanning errors corrected in headings: AEQVAEUUB = aequaevus, PATEIS = PATRIS, SPIBITUM = SPIRITUM. In 1.6.2 'fitetur' read as 'fatetur' (confesses). In 1.6.1 the punctuation 'dum unus. dicit et non unus facit' is taken as 'dum unus dicit et non unus facit'.

The heading of ch. VIIII is badly scanned (OBESSS, SPIIUTUS, INGBNITUS, UIDBATUR, OBNITUS); read as 'non obesse sancti spiritus deitati quod nec ingenitus uideatur esse nec genitus'. In 1.8.1 'uidene' is taken as 'see whether'; the subject (Scripture) is supplied. 'Quis appendit tribus digitis molem terrae' follows the Old Latin form of Isa. 40:12.

11.3: 'humo erit confusa diuinitas' is evidently corrupt; translated as if 'una erit confusa diuinitas' ('the divinity will be one confused [whole]'). The following clause on an essence 'intermediate between substance and persons' is obscure and is rendered literally. 11.ab1: 'ACTIBUS APOSTOLORUK ADBERTIO' read as 'apostolorum adsertio'.

13.1: the text's 'dabit nobis' is evidently a misprint for 'uobis' ("you"), translated so. 13.2: 'quanti ad crinem purpurei splendoris aspexerint' is awkward (repeated 'quanti ad'); the text may be corrupt; 'crinem' taken as the flame's 'tress'. 13.3: 'ab aquilone et mari' (from the north and the sea) echoes the biblical formula, where 'sea' stands for the west. 13.5: 'uenit descendamus' read as 'uenite' (come). 2.1.1: '(nationes)' is an editorial supplement in the edition.

2.1.3 'de proditione est coniuentiae': sense uncertain; taken as the soul's own betrayal by consent. 2.2.1 'ante creationis initia' taken as referring to the forming of Christ's humanity. 2.2.2 'unde uidebitur, incipiat' read as 'let him begin from where it seems good'; the bracketed '[de testimoniis]' is the edition's. 'siue dubio' read as 'sine dubio'. 2.3.1 'quem cum patre et filio eiusdem honoris et gloriae': the punctuation could also be read differently but the sense is unaffected. 2.3.2 'archaugelis' read as 'archangelis'.

2.4.3: 'me uero infidelium corda ... non credunt' is grammatically incomplete (a verb governing 'me' seems lost, e.g. 'do not receive'); translated as the sense allows. 2.4.6: the text has 'in ipso' and once 'in ipsum'; rendered uniformly 'in him'. 2.4.1 'fac gradum' taken as 'make a step of rank', i.e. introduce a gradation.

Heading of ch. V: 'KEMATUS' read as 'renatus'. In 2.7.1 the text has '001 diuina', a scanning corruption; a noun such as 'scriptura' or 'auctoritas' seems to have dropped out, translated as 'divine [Scripture]'. In 2.7.2 'adierit' read as 'adicit' (adds) and 'uoueris' as 'noueris' (know). In 2.7.3 'nos autem baptizabimini' read as 'uos autem'. In 2.7.2 the Psalm verse 'audiam, quid loquatur in me' follows this text's wording ('in me').

2.7.4: 'abremissa' read as 'remissa' (remission). 2.8.1: the stray period in 'praeparare. merentur' is ignored, reading 'qui ei se praeparare merentur in templum, dei utique, non creaturae'. The sentence 'in creatorem peccat ... addicat' is taken as a rhetorical question, which the following 'non ita est' answers. 2.9 heading: 'PBR' read as 'PER'. 2.10.1: the author introduces the Hebrews quotation (Heb 2:4) although he announces Corinthians. 2.11.1: 'sicut deus diuisit mensuram fidei' is actually Rom 12:3, though the author ascribes it to Corinthians.

'corpora uestra templum est' (plural subject, singular verb) is kept as in the text. The sentence 'ergo qui ... possidemur' is loosely constructed; it is rendered as two clauses joined by a semicolon. 'naturae debitis exuere' is taken as stripping them of the debts owed by [fallen] nature; the sense is somewhat uncertain.

nodes.text: CHAPTER HEADINGS OF THE FIRST BOOK.
I. That the Holy Spirit is to be understood wholly and openly [as God] from the head of the faith, that is, from the creed.
II. That we ought not to believe in the Church as in the Holy Spirit, but, with the preposition "in" removed, [we ought to believe] the catholic Church.
III. That Christ was not begotten by the Holy Spirit, as by God, but created.
IV. On the unity [of God], to be affirmed by prophetic testimonies.
V. On the Trinity, and that even the liberal disciplines held a view about three persons.
VI. When the Son is called the face of the Father, he is recognised as coeternal with the Father.
VII. That the Spirit of the Father is himself the Holy Spirit.
VIII. On the finger of God.
IX. That it does not detract from the deity of the Holy Spirit that he appears to be neither unbegotten nor begotten.
X. That the Holy Spirit is the bestower of perfect gifts of grace.
XI. From the Acts of the Apostles the affirmation of the Trinity is repeated, where it is also affirmed, against the Novatians, that Christ was sent to grant repentance.
XII. That it is proper to God to sanctify the creature.
XIII. That the Holy Spirit is not confined to a place.
THE FIRST BOOK.
THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT IS TO BE UNDERSTOOD WHOLLY AND OPENLY [AS GOD] FROM THE HEAD OF THE FAITH, THAT IS, FROM THE CREED.

The catholic faith has been spread through the whole world by the patriarchs and prophets and the dispensers of grace, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit. The care and perfection of the apostles, just as they had spread it abroad through the sacred pages, so gathered it with wonderful brevity into the saving formula of the creed, and, as it were, arranged scattered kinds of remedies into one body, and, as if from countless spices, made a precious ointment, whose scent has filled all the ends of the earth with the power of its spiritual fragrance, so that in the very assent of all the strength of the truth may appear.

And since we must repeat to those who err, as to little children and the ignorant, the first elements of the Christian tradition, in this perfection of the creed both the unity and the Trinity are plainly disclosed, when the confession, repeated three times, renders one homage of belief to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. In these words also the sacred number of three hundred and eighteen bishops condemned the emerging error of Arius and Macedonius, [saying]: I believe in God the Father, I believe in his only Son our Lord, I believe also in the Holy Spirit. For even if the frailty of a few out of that number fell away from this, it did not undo the mystery of the whole number. And we have called it a sacred number for this reason: because three hundred, in Greek numerals or reckoning, shows the sign of the cross, and eighteen the adorable name of Jesus. In this number and mystery, then, in which holy Abraham too triumphed over countless nations, the piety of the elders confounded the enemy of the faith under the one proclamation of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Hence it must also be understood that those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit under eternal damnation were either baptised without the full creed, or lied to themselves in that very creed and font, before which every person, renouncing the devil, confesses: I believe also in the Holy Spirit.

I believe, I say, also in the Holy Spirit. Let us recognise the special privilege of this very phrase. You may believe any man whatever; but know that you ought to believe in [someone] only for the divine majesty. But even this is one thing, to believe God, and another, to believe in God. Even the devil is said to believe that God exists, according to the apostle: for the demons also believe and tremble. But no one is shown to believe in God unless he has piously hoped in him. To believe in God, then, is this: faithfully to seek him and to pass over into him with all one's love. So "I believe in him" is to say: I confess him, I worship him, I adore him, I hand over and pour my whole self into his right and lordship. In the reverence of this profession all the homage owed to the divine name is contained.
II. THAT WE OUGHT NOT TO BELIEVE IN THE CHURCH AS IN THE HOLY SPIRIT, BUT, WITH THE PREPOSITION "IN" REMOVED, [WE OUGHT TO BELIEVE] THE CATHOLIC CHURCH.

But you object and say that God cannot at once be shown by this phrase in which we say: I believe also in the Holy Spirit, because there follows: I believe in the holy catholic Church. First, I do not know how Macedonius dares to name the catholic Church, he who, outside the catholic [Church], has been shut out, an exile from salvation, having become one of the number of those of whom it is said: the wicked will walk round about. So you say: I believe in the holy catholic Church. Why, by slipping in something tiny, that is, the syllable "in", do you try to weave in a vast darkness? We believe the Church as the mother of regeneration; we do not believe in the Church as in the author of salvation. For since the whole Church confesses this of the Holy Spirit, can the Church also believe in itself? Therefore, since the teaching of the fathers mentioned, celebrated throughout the whole world, confirms that one must believe specially in the Trinity alone, either remove this syllable from the name of the Church, or else establish from the Scriptures by a clear profession that you believe in the Church: teach it by testimonies, prove it by divine oracles, setting aside the presumption of your own words.

Let us take what is to be believed entirely from the sacred books, from whose spring the very sequence of the creed is derived and stands. Whoever believes in the Church believes in a human being. For man did not begin to exist from the Church, but the Church from man. Turn away, therefore, from this blasphemous persuasion, that you should think you ought to believe in any human creature, since one is not to believe at all either in an angel or in an archangel. For these things which follow in the creed after the name of the Holy Spirit look to the close of the creed with the preposition "in" removed, so that we believe the holy Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, eternal life, [while believing] in God, that is, so that we confess that these things were ordained by God and stand firm in God. For the inexperience of some has dragged and snatched this preposition, as it were from the nearest and neighbouring clause, into the following one, and has imprudently added it superfluously. But in none of the canonical [Scriptures], on which the text of the creed depends, do we find that we ought to believe in the Church as in the Holy Spirit and the Son. And therefore, as to the Holy Spirit, since every creature is a stranger to this honour, he in whom we are commanded to believe is God. This expression the voice of the Lord and Saviour assigns specially to the divinity, saying thus: believe in God, and believe in me; and again: whoever believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me.
III. THAT CHRIST WAS NOT BEGOTTEN BY THE HOLY SPIRIT, AS BY GOD, BUT CREATED.

But since the catholic Church confesses: conceived of the Holy Spirit, the Macedonians must be asked at this point whether they consider the Holy Spirit the creator or the father of the Redeemer. If perhaps they answer "father", since at the beginning of the creed they have already said: I believe in God the Father almighty, they will confusedly confess that he has two fathers. But if they affirm "creator", as the truth holds, they will be forced, even by necessity, to proclaim with us [that he is] the Lord of all. And so through the prophet Isaiah, as through his trumpet and from his temple, he speaks, foreshadowing the two substances in Christ: drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the just one; let the earth be opened and bud forth the Saviour; I the Lord have created him. For the man assumed from Mary was the work of the Holy Spirit, not a portion [of him], nor begotten by him, but created. He was conceived by power, not by substance; by operation, not by participation; by might, not by descent.
IV. ON THE UNITY [OF GOD], TO BE AFFIRMED BY PROPHETIC TESTIMONIES.

The catholic faith venerates a threefold majesty under the confession of one divinity [hear the one divinity from the sacred books]: hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God; and: you shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone; and again: I am the Lord, and there is no God besides me; and in the Psalms: you who do wonders, you alone are God; likewise: you alone are most high over all the earth. Through Isaiah also: God of Israel, who sit upon the cherubim, you alone are God of all the kingdoms of the earth; likewise: I the Lord, I am the first and the last; likewise: I am the Lord, that is my name; my glory I will not give to another. And so that you may know that this testimony, that is, "first and last", pertains to Christ, he said of himself in another place: I am the beginning, who also speak to you; likewise: before me there was no God, and after me there will be none; I am the Lord, and apart from me there is no saviour, which pertains specially to Christ, the Saviour of the human race; likewise: thus says the Lord, your redeemer, who formed you from the womb: I am the Lord who makes all things, who stretches out the heavens, who alone establishes the earth, and no one is with me. This refers properly to Jesus, maker and redeemer, of whom the evangelist records: all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made; likewise: there is no other God apart from me, and there is no saviour besides me; likewise: I am the first and I am the last, my hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens, just as Jesus Christ in another place plainly affirms of himself, saying: I [am] the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. In these testimonies the Holy Spirit is also included, and in them the unity of the divine substance is to be confessed concerning the Holy Spirit in such a way that one must believe there is also in them the distinct property of the persons and an undivided plurality.
V. ON THE TRINITY, AND THAT THE LIBERAL DISCIPLINES TOO HAVE PERCEIVED THREE PERSONS.

So by the words of God we have shown one deity; let us now teach three in one deity: three names, not three kingdoms; three appellations, but not three powers; three essences or subsistences, but not three substances. It is clear that even worldly wisdom has understood that the whole multitude of the ages is enclosed within the scheme of three persons. Which are these three? That is: I, you, he. Therefore, as we have said, even the liberal studies, having borrowed instruction from the spiritual disciplines, perceived that there are only three persons in things, and it appeared plainly to them that neither does the second person suffice for completeness nor can the third be surpassed, because fullness, tending towards the third number, shows duality to be half-full, while perfection, completed in three, rejects a fourth. Having passed over these things with brief mention, let us rather affirm by sacred testimonies that the Trinity subsists in unity.

But you say: why do you bring before me the words "unity" and "trinity", which you do not find in the canonical reading? It is no wonder if he who does not deserve to enter the inner chambers of salvation is terrified by, and flees from, even the door of truth. For what is so near, so natural, so proper, as that from "one" there should be named "unity", and from "three" "trinity", by the catholic definitions of the fathers? Words that depend on what precedes them are not to be examined by themselves, nor indeed does it follow that those should be judged foreign which are born from "one" and "three", that is, from the property of an evident origin. Notice that each of these terms is not presumptuous but derivative. These words antiquity found from the time of the primitive Church, authority brought forward, and long age confirmed.
VI. WHILE THE SON IS CALLED THE FACE OF THE FATHER, HE IS RECOGNISED AS COEVAL WITH THE FATHER.

Receive the Trinity from the sacred volumes: in the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters. The Father is the author, the Son the coeval beginning, the Holy Spirit poured over the waters. So he was borne over the waters with the eminence of one who rules, even then, I believe, prefiguring the gifts of baptism. In the making of man, too, the threefold repetition of the deity shows that it is the work not of one but of three persons. For so we read: and God said: let us make man in our image and likeness. Notice the sentence, single in its statement, multiple in its reply. And God said: let us make man. What else is this but that the substance of unity speaks and the power of the Trinity works? Observe how the name of God is pronounced three times in the creation of man. For so we have in Genesis: and God said: let us make man; and again: God created man; and a third time: God blessed him. God said, God made, God blessed. Because of the three persons the one divinity is repeated three times. In this place understand plainly also the mystery of unity. See, the image and likeness of God is given to each man by three, and yet it is recognised to be one. God said: let us make. Attend carefully: while one speaks and not one makes, and while again he mingles the plural with the singular and does not say "in our images and likenesses", or indeed "in my image and likeness", he commends unity by the singular, the Trinity by the plural. So in saying "let us make in our" the number of persons is set out, but in saying in the singular "in the image and likeness" the undivided deity is gathered into one substance.

When God had appeared to Abraham at the door of his tent, and from one, three had wonderfully presented themselves to his eyes, he, aware of the majesty, worshipped one in three. In the psalms too the unity is plainly designated with its persons: do not cast me away, he says, from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. See, the prophet, supplicating the Father, dreads offending the Holy Spirit no less than the Father and the Son. Do not cast me away, he says, from your face. The Son, as he is the image of the Father, so too is taken as the face of the Father. And so we read: Philip, he who sees me sees the Father also; likewise: where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? Notice, faithless one, the mystery of the Trinity in a perfect confession. The prophet speaks to the Father, confesses the Son as the face of the Father, and also declares the Holy Spirit poured out through all things. Concerning the Son, moreover, the Lord also speaks to Moses: my face shall go before you. This name, that is "face", pertains both to the unity of substance and to the coeternity of majesty. As for their thinking him lesser because he was born: what is it for God to be born of God, except to have come forth from God by nature? But you say: if he is from him, he is younger than him. See, the arm is born from the body and the face from its head, and yet it is agreed that the face is not younger than its head, nor the arm later than its body. If, then, any head was ever older than its face, then presume to assert that the Father is older than his image, which consists in the perfect likeness and equality of Christ. So the Son cannot be distinguished from the Father either in power or in time, just as a face cannot be separated from the head, nor in any way be found younger than its head.
VII. THAT THE SPIRIT OF THE FATHER IS THE HOLY SPIRIT HIMSELF.

But you say: show me that the Holy Spirit subsists in his own essence. Wherever and however often I read either "the Spirit of the Father" or "my Spirit" or "the Spirit of God", I see, you say, that it is to be referred not to the person of the Holy Spirit but to that of the Father. Here first they pile up the blasphemy of their impiety, since they say that the Holy Spirit of God must be believed to be one or the other: either a creature, or indeed the Father himself. Deservedly he who does not confess the Holy Spirit is carried down with confused mind even to an insult against the Father. Certainly, if he is a thing made, he cannot belong to the substance of the Father. But if you think him the Father's power, how do you presume to lower him to the insult of being a thing made? We, however, will show by evident testimonies that "the Spirit of God" is said not of the Father but properly of the Holy Spirit.

We read in Isaiah that upon the Lord Jesus descended the Spirit of the Lord, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety. Of this Spirit of the Lord, then, who descended upon the Saviour in a sacred descent, the Son says through Isaiah: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me; and the evangelist Matthew: see, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending upon him like a dove. And that this Spirit of God, whom the Saviour received in baptism, is the Holy Spirit, the evangelist Luke has clearly taught, saying: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan. We read in the prophet Joel: in those days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh. That what he says, "of my Spirit", was said of the Holy Spirit is clear, because when the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles at the sacred solemnity of Pentecost, the apostle Peter then took up this testimony from the prophet.

Moreover, the Gospels have taught, in differing words but with concordant truth, that the Spirit of the Father is the Holy Spirit himself. For when Matthew said: for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you, Mark explained openly that this Spirit of the Father is the Holy Spirit, saying: whatever is given you in that hour, speak that; for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. And Luke likewise showed that this Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit, saying: do not be anxious how or what you shall say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that hour what you ought to say. According to these, then, whenever you read either "the Spirit of the Father" or "the Spirit of God", you must, laying aside your error, confess that it is to be referred specially to the Holy Spirit. Likewise Isaiah too counts the Holy Spirit as one in the glory of the Trinity when he says: I saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne, and the Seraphim stood and cried one to another: holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth. And next he says: and I heard the voice of the Lord saying: go and say to this people: by hearing you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will see and not see. Who this Lord of Sabaoth was, who was seen by the prophet through an assumed appearance, or who spoke in the prophet, Paul shows in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: well did the Holy Spirit speak through the prophet Isaiah to our fathers: by hearing you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will see and not see.

Let us at least believe Paul, the most celebrated herald of truth, that the Holy Spirit was that Lord of hosts whom Isaiah saw and who spoke through Isaiah. But since "holy, holy, holy" resounds in threefold repetition, let us see whether this honour does not refer to the whole Trinity. Isaiah, when he says: I saw the Lord of Sabaoth, is recognised by the Jews as proclaiming the Father. The evangelist John is shown openly to assert the Son, saying thus: therefore they could not believe in Jesus, because Isaiah said: he has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart. These things Isaiah said when he saw the glory of the Son of God and spoke of him. And as for what the same Isaiah says: and I heard the voice of the Lord saying: go and say to this people: seeing you will see and not see, the apostle Paul, as we have said, confirms that this Lord is the Holy Spirit. You see, then, that "holy, holy, holy", this cry celebrates the whole Trinity together; and just as in these three words there is no unlikeness and no difference, so in the power of the Trinity there can be no distance.
VIII. ON THE FINGER OF GOD.

But you say: from this it is evidently recognised that the Holy Spirit is lesser, because he is called the finger of God. It is not so. But when you hear it said of the Holy Spirit: if I by the finger of God cast out demons, know that it shows not a diminution of glory but the unity of substance, and not a disparity of honour but a concord of work. What then? Because the Holy Spirit is sometimes called the finger [of God], is he therefore believed to be less than the Son and the Father? Flee the error of this persuasion, and see whether at times in this designation of a finger [Scripture] does not include both the Father and the Son. Let us remember that it was not said of one finger when we read: for I will see your heavens, the works of your fingers. But you say that in "fingers" only the Son and the Holy Spirit are signified, under a kind of duality. Lest you try to assert this of two persons, in another place Isaiah speaks of the Trinity by the number of three fingers only, saying: who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers? What is more evident concerning the unity of the Trinity, what clearer? Has he not here, in three fingers, weighed the equality of one power on a kind of balance of mystery? Therefore, as has been said, since you have now been instructed about the partnership in work, do not doubt the parity of power. In saying, then: who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers, he wished here specially to speak of the cooperation of power and of the unity of substance, which is shown to be one and the same in the three fingers.

But nonetheless, notice in the prophet Isaiah the proper person of the Holy Spirit within the distinction of the Trinity, where the Son, saying of himself: I am the first and I am the last, went on to add: and now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit. One, then, in person is God the Father, another the Spirit of God the Father. And so, when the Son is read to be sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit, it is evidently disclosed that, under the name of three persons, the Holy Spirit subsists in himself; just as in another place the same prophet distinguishes the being of the Trinity: behold my servant, I will uphold him, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased; I have put my Spirit upon him. The Father calls the Son his beloved servant, upon whom he has put his Spirit, of which Jesus Christ testifies with his own voice: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me. And so that it might be manifest even to the Gentiles, [there is] that word of the Gospel: go, he says, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, where under three persons he asserts one work and one name, an undivided majesty. We have, as has been said, according to Luke: and when Jesus had been baptized, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove, and a voice came from heaven: you are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased. The Son, then, is declared in the body, the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, the Father in the voice. But in this place the form in the dove is to be understood as passing, not as an abiding substance.
VIIII. THAT IT DOES NOT HARM THE DEITY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT THAT HE IS SEEN TO BE NEITHER UNBEGOTTEN NOR BEGOTTEN.

But meanwhile, since we show the proper person of the Holy Spirit and confess the Father unbegotten, and acknowledge the Son as only-begotten, you ask me whether the Holy Spirit is to be confessed unbegotten or begotten or something else. The holy Scriptures speak of the power and deity of the Holy Spirit; whether he should be called begotten or unbegotten, they do not say. See what darkness unbelief makes for itself. You do not want to know what God did not want to be unknown, and you want to know what he did not command to be inquired into. He did not say "begotten", lest you believe him the Son; he did not say "unbegotten", lest you think him the Father; but, to distinguish his being, he testified that he proceeds from the Father, as we read: the Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father. This being so, at least in this way acknowledge that the Holy Spirit has his own person. The difference of name proves that there is a third besides the two; the unity of majesty shows that he who proceeds from God is not third in order or rank. For he who comes forth from the inmost being of God is shown to be not a creature of God but the substance of God. Do not search out how he is God, whom it is manifest is God. Here the reason is hidden; the truth is not hidden. Why ask how he is the partner and equal of the king, who is agreed to be of royal honour and royal stock? Inquiry about the name is superfluous where there is no doubt about the sublimity. Therefore, because the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, [Scripture] says: but whoever does not have the Spirit of the Lord does not belong to him; and in another place: he breathed on them and said: receive the Holy Spirit.

You ask whether he is unbegotten or begotten. The sacred oracles have sung nothing on this; it is impious to break in upon the divine silences. What God did not think should be indicated in his Scriptures, he did not wish you to ask or know through superfluous curiosity. He judged that what pertains to your salvation should reach your understanding. What we must believe about the Holy Spirit, let us consult the holy oracles. For this very thing, that he calls the Son begotten, would you dare to say it unless you had learned it from the heavenly attestation of the Scriptures? Or would you presume to assert that Christ the Lord was either born of a virgin or begotten of a Father of equal age and coeternal, unless you had taken it from reading, unless you had consulted the divine words about God? And so, how you ought to think about the Holy Spirit, you must return to the apostles and the Gospels, with whom and in whom you do not doubt that God has spoken.

To return, then, to your pointless proposition: does the glory or substance of the Holy Spirit depend on this, whether he is shown to be unbegotten or begotten? For it detracts nothing from the Son that he is not read to be unbegotten, nor from the Father that he is not held to be begotten. In such terms there is a propriety of designation, not a difference of power or majesty. Begotten and unbegotten is a difference of person, not of nature. When, then, you have said or heard useless and unnecessary things about begotten and unbegotten, suited only to cavilling, will you be content to stop at that point? Surely you will still ask whether he is God. But when you have learned from what is read that he is God, you will then have nothing to ask, because once you begin to know what is strong and complete, you will have no need to inquire into what is empty and void. Where, then, the reason of usefulness and the fullness of truth is understood to be, there let the striving for salvation tend.
X. THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT IS THE BESTOWER OF THE PERFECT GIFTS OF GRACE.

That the Holy Spirit is the bestower of heavenly gifts of grace and the dispenser of sanctifications, the very meaning of his name declares. And his magnificence was made manifest even in the Old Testament. For there his grace was granted only to certain chosen ones, that is, to patriarchs and prophets alike and to the holy and elect, so that through the very perfection of the gifts I may understand the dignity of the giver. But as far as is most clearly discerned in the holy Scriptures, the Father works some things himself through himself, some specially through the Son, some through the Holy Spirit, though under the privilege of a common power. That we exist seems properly to be referred to the Father, in whom, as the apostle said, we live and move and are. That we are capable of reason and wisdom and justice is assigned specially to him who is reason and wisdom and justice, that is, to the Son. And that, being called, we are regenerated, and, regenerated, are renewed, and, renewed, are sanctified, is by the divine oracles evidently ascribed to the person of the Holy Spirit.

But the sacred pages speak of these things under the distinction of the undivided Trinity in such a way that, however much a difference of work appears in each, unity of will still remains in the three. So both Gentiles and catechumens share in the dispensation of the Father and the Son, but in the sanctification and infusion of the Holy Spirit not readily, except those who have already received baptism, been purified and made spiritual, apostolic men too and apostles, and those prepared with their whole spirit for martyrdom. And amid all this, will he still be judged a creature by the impious, who within the undivided Trinity, in the ordering of human salvation, is allotted all the more magnificent and more perfect gifts? But perhaps you say: then the Holy Spirit is greater, whose works are greater and nobler. It is not so. For it is the custom of the Trinity that to whichever person it commits the office of administering a matter, to him it ascribes the effect of its accomplishment; and so the work may perhaps be different, but the purpose common. And if there is a special deed in each, a general counsel remains in the three; and therefore, even if they have a distinct task in operation, they nevertheless hold one consent in ordering.

After the ascension of the Lord, the Holy Spirit is described as having descended to heap up and fulfil his benefits, of whom the Saviour himself speaks through the Gospel of John: that Spirit of truth, whom the Father will send in my name. The Father, he says, will send in my name: evidently of the Trinity. Of what creature have we ever read or heard it said that it came into this world in the name of God? This one, then, of whom Christ the Lord God says: unless I go, the Paraclete will not come to you, is without doubt God, who is sent in the place of God to confirm the gifts of God. In these two sayings, under the distinction of the Trinity, the person of the Holy Spirit too is plainly declared. Not without reason, therefore, is this also referred to the equality of divinity, that just as the Son, so also the Holy Spirit is called Paraclete in the Scriptures. And how can we prove this? Certainly from the authority of the apostle John, when he says: if any of us, he says, has sinned, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ, and he is the propitiation for our sins. Paraclete, that is, advocate, which refers to the person of the Son, or also comforter, which pertains to the Holy Spirit: one expression of the Greek language signifies both. In the Gospel of John we have: and I, he says, will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete. Another Paraclete, that is, of like power, of equal glory and of the same nature. And another Paraclete: if you think the Holy Spirit is one of the creatures, it is unworthy that at his descent a creature should confirm the benefits that the Creator conferred, and that, as if the power of the maker had been ineffective, the completion of an unfinished work, as it were, should be reserved to a creature, however more excellent.

You, then, heap abuse on the Holy Spirit as a creature, though the Son of God, by divine testimony from his own utterance, made himself equal to him. And another Paraclete: here, in a twofold sense, recognise both the distinction of person and the equality of substance. Here perhaps you may object: Christ seems to have made himself equal, under the name of Paraclete, to the Holy Spirit, who is certainly the material and the handiwork of God's work, because Jesus himself too is shown to have been created from Mary. This argument is as weak as it is faithless. For if you think Christ was likened to the Paraclete according to his humanity, not even this agrees with the truth. For, made a little lower than the angels and become one of us, he could not be compared to the first, heavenly and, as you claim, more excellent creature. But if Christ said this according to the form of God, it is certain that the handiwork ought not to have been compared with the maker. And so, if as man he makes himself equal to this more excellent creature, it is the pride of the lesser; if as God, it is an insult to the greater. Since, then, this comparison is not recognised as consistent within the condition of a creature, it remains that both be believed to be God and that the equality of divinity be compared between them mutually. For when the Saviour speaks through John: and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive, he who can be given to the whole world is manifestly the God of the world. Here too recognise the threefold Trinity. It is the Father who is indicated as the one to be asked, the Son who is understood as the one who will ask, the Holy Spirit who is promised as the one to be sent by the Father. Notice that the person of the Holy Spirit is not so much associated with creatures as his kin, as you claim, but is in all things joined to the Trinity in works and made equal in powers.
XI. In the Acts of the Apostles the assertion of the Trinity is repeated, where Christ also is affirmed, against the Novatians, to have been sent to grant repentance.

In the Acts of the Apostles Peter, discoursing about the Lord Jesus, speaks thus: being therefore exalted by the right hand of God and having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he has poured out this which you see and hear. In the right hand the Son, in God the Father, in the proper sense of his own name the Holy Spirit is designated. And in what follows we read: then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, by this name this man stands before you whole. Look here too at the distinction of the Trinity expressed. Peter, bearing the Holy Spirit within himself, speaks of the Son dying in the flesh and the Father raising him. There, likewise, it is repeated in an apostolic utterance: and now, it says, Lord, look upon their threats; and: they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with boldness. Notice in this place too that the Holy Spirit is contained in the Trinity. In the prayer the Father is asked, in the word of God the Son is recognised, in the steadfastness of the apostles the fire of the Holy Spirit is at work. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit. It belongs to manifest majesty to be able to pour itself into very many at once by the subtlety of incorporeal divinity, and to remain whole without loss. Likewise, when the apostles had said of Jesus: him God exalted with his right hand as prince and saviour, to grant repentance in Israel for the remission of sins. We, it says, are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to all who obey him. Understand here that, in the order of the Trinity, the Son is appointed by the Father not only to preach but to grant repentance, and that the Holy Spirit is poured into those who comply, to reward their obedience.

Stephen is filled with the Holy Spirit at the moment of his passion, and, the gates of righteousness being opened to him, the Son is revealed at the right hand of the Father, as he himself, filled with the Holy Spirit, declares: behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. See how he performed the offices of his passion in the sight of the Trinity. Peter addresses the centurion Cornelius, saying: Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit. God anointed, that is, power filled [him], blessing was poured into [him], divinity penetrated [him]. How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit. Three things here evidently stand out in their proper characters: the gift, the giver, the one gifted; the anointer, the anointed, the ointment; as the divine word also says in another place: God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness. In the man assumed God is anointed and God anoints, and in the descent of the heavenly dove the power of the Father is recognised. It is not right that this Holy Spirit, by whom Christ the Son of Man, already full as Son of God, is filled, should be believed to be anything other than God. For if he were a creature, how could he penetrate the incorporeal nature that penetrates all things? For the Trinity has room for itself, as we have: I am in the Father and the Father in me; and again: the Spirit searches even the depths of God; likewise: the Spirit, who proceeds from the Father. Unless this Holy Spirit were from the Father and dwelt in him by nature, poured into the inner being of the Father, he could not proceed from the Father.

But you ask whether the Spirit always proceeds from the Father. Always with him, always from him, as heat from fire, so he is brought forth without interruption, so that he knows how to go forth and does not know how to be separated. For if the procession of the Holy Spirit were not everlasting, his substance would seem to be local. If incorporeal brightness, which has room for itself, does not penetrate each into the other without mingling of itself, then the divinity will be one confused [whole]. For mingling takes away the distinct property of the threefold essence, while mutual infusion shows a distinct essence, which can be seen as intermediate between substance and persons. To substance belongs that it subsists; to the persons belongs that each subsists properly in itself. Paul addresses his disciples, saying: I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has set you as bishops to rule the church of God, which he acquired with his own blood. How clearly the whole Trinity is designated in its persons! He declares the counsel of God the Father, he affirms that the bishops were ordained by the Holy Spirit, and he shows that Christ too, by whose blood the church was acquired, is God.

To the Romans also the Trinity is set out under the proper sense of the names: but if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you. The Father raises, the Son is raised, and because of the indwelling Spirit life is promised to the mortal bodies that are to be raised again. And in what follows: but you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. When he says the Spirit of God and then the Spirit of Christ, notice that here he designates the person of Christ under the name of God. Or if here he signifies the Father, whose Spirit he is, under the name of God, see: here the Holy Spirit is declared, through unity of substance, to be the Spirit of both the Father and the Son, and is rightly discerned to proceed from both, and is perceived to have a distinct person in the bond of the Trinity; and whoever does not have the Holy Spirit is shown not to have Christ either. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is God; when he is denied, Christ too is denied; and since he said: no one comes to the Father except through me, whoever is empty of the Holy Spirit is not Christ's and has lost the way by which one comes to the Father.
XII. That it is proper to God to sanctify the creature.

To the Corinthians, the first: and such indeed you were, but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. See, here too, under the mention of our God, that is, of the Father, the Holy Spirit, with Christ cooperating, sanctifies the faithful of the Corinthians. No creature can at all sanctify another; the bestowal of sanctification is the munificence of majesty alone. In this place, in the name of Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God, recognise three persons. To the Corinthians, the second: the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. The grace of Christ, the love of God, the fellowship of the Holy Spirit evidently expressed three persons. Likewise to the Corinthians, the second: but he who confirms us with you in Christ and who anointed us is God, and who sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. See in the works the unity of the undivided Trinity. The Father confirms and seals us through Christ, and, being about to give himself, already gives in the present, through himself, the Holy Spirit as a pledge. In earthly business the amount of a deposit is a certain portion of the contract for which it was given, but the value of a pledge exceeds the worth of the thing for which it is laid down. Here, however, his pledge must be equal to the majesty, since it cannot be preferred above it. For what is perfect cannot be surpassed; so the Father grants the pledge of the Holy Spirit on his own behalf. Let nothing, then, in the Holy Spirit be thought half-full, since he is compared to fullness. For it is not right that he who is given in the place of a pledge, standing for God, should be believed to be anything other than God. Likewise to Titus: he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ. See, here too, in the manifest Trinity, the Father pours out through the Son the abundance of the Holy Spirit, and, what must be especially noticed, he ascribes to the Holy Spirit himself the power of regeneration and renewal. Peter too in his letter sets out the Trinity as inseparable in its persons, saying: according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, may grace and peace be multiplied to you. In the foreknowledge the Father, in the sanctification the Holy Spirit, in the sprinkling of the blood Christ is shown.
XIII. That the Holy Spirit is not confined to a place.

Let us show from his powers and works that the Holy Spirit is God. Every creature, just as it is subject to beginnings in time, also knows that it is confined to a place, bounded by fixed spaces and limits. The Holy Spirit is enclosed by no boundaries, as a thing made would be; he must be held to be God because of the very freedom of his diffused majesty. The voice of the Lord and Saviour to the apostles is: the Father, he says, will give you the Spirit of truth, to be with you for ever. If he is confined to a place and remained in them perpetually, he certainly could not be anywhere else. Let us see whether his nature is bounded by local limits. The Lord says to the apostles: you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judaea and Samaria and to the end of the earth. After his ascension the Holy Spirit came upon them, and there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it sat upon each one of them.

Let us see why the blessings of different tongues are given first: no doubt so that they might be made fit for the instruction of the faithful peoples. And as for its being recorded that it sat upon each one, the reason is so that it may be understood that he was not divided among the many, but remained whole in each one, as is usual with fires. For a kindled fire, as we know, has this nature: to as many as look upon it, upon the tress of its purple brightness, to so many it imparts the use of its light, to so many it grants the service of its gift, and it nonetheless remains in its own wholeness. So the power of the Holy Spirit, however much it flows out, however abundantly the grace of the divine generosity overflows into very many, just as it is shown to admit no measure, so it suffers no expenditure. Notice God from the dignity of the works. The apostles, full of the Holy Spirit, about to dispense the treasures of salvation through the whole world, carry this heavenly gift about in themselves and pass it on to others by the laying on of hands. The gain of the receiver comes about without loss to the giver; he is handed over whole to those who believe and is possessed whole by those who hand him on; by his infusion the whole world is filled; he is extended without being thinned, spread abroad without being divided.

Especially on that most holy night of regeneration, from east to west, from the rising of the sun to its setting, from the north and from the sea, everywhere the same one and full Spirit is at work; he is believed to be present through all things by invocation, he is felt by blessing; countless multitudes are washed in one baptism and, as the apostle said, are given to drink of one Spirit, and are reborn into the one bosom of him who adopts [them]. And therefore God says: in those days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh [notice that he said: I will pour out of my Spirit] and he did not say: I will pour out my Spirit; that is: I will dispense of him as much as the world can receive. You see that he goes forth from the Father and yet is not separated from the Father; he is sent and not lost; he is poured out and retained; and in his being read to be poured out, the greatness of his fullness is declared. The book of Genesis testifies at the beginning of the sacred volume: but the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters. He was borne, it says, over the waters. The very word seems to assign [to him] the abundance of one who fills all things and the eminence of one who rules. The prophet too celebrates with like testimony this magnificence of his, circumscribed by no spaces of place, saying: where shall I go from your Spirit? That is, where shall I hide myself from the sight of him who, I do not doubt, is present through all things, that is, within and without; whose eye, penetrating the abysses, I dread within the secret of my breast; to whose presence I know all things that he founded are subject; about whom, since he is a consuming fire, I clearly understand it was said: nor is there anyone who can hide himself from his heat; whose ineffable greatness enters, fills and exceeds the depths of the underworld, the expanse of the waves, the extent of the lands, the heights of the heavens.

He is said to be sent by the Father and the Son, and is known to proceed from their substance and to do one work with them; and for this reason the Son says of him: the Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father. He did not say: he was created by the Father, but: he proceeds from the Father, that is, from fellowship in the Father's power and from the property of [his] nature. But from the very word, when he is said to proceed from the Father, it is shown that he has no beginning, [being] with the Father. What is it, then, that the Son is said to be born of God the Father, and the Holy Spirit is signified to proceed? If you ask what difference there is between one being born and one proceeding, the difference is clearly this: that the one is born from one, the other goes forth from both. That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, then, shows three privileges of deity in him: namely, that he is proved to subsist in his own person, to abide without any interval of time, and to exist wholly from the substance of the Father. When, therefore, he is said to proceed, by the very property of the word he is known to be circumscribed by no laws of time, but to lack beginning and end. And since we read: I am who am, and: he who is has sent me, 'proceeds' likewise indicates this. For 'to be' and 'to proceed' are the expression of one and the same eternity. Therefore the procession itself, touching neither a first nor a last, is understood to be subject to no beginning or end.

Let us not, then, believe him to be confined to a place because we gather from Scripture that he is sent by the Father; for of the Father and the Son too we read that they descend and come as if by some motion. Let us see where. I, he says, and my Father will come and make our dwelling with him. And again, when the giants were striving to raise a tower to heaven, the person of the Father speaks: come, let us go down and confound their tongues. Here, then, through the sounds of our words the effecting of things is shown to our senses. But divine power does not admit local motion: it neither arrives by a driving course nor departs by a gliding return. For he who exceeds all things, where does he withdraw to? Of the Holy Spirit we have learned from sacred Scripture: but the church had peace throughout all Judaea, walking in the fear of God, and was filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit. And how, in the face of these things, does anyone presume to assert that he is a creature confined to a place, who is proved to fill the church of an infinite multitude, so that it is plain that what the apostle says also belongs to him: the Father of mercies and God of all consolation? We have in the psalm: the rush of the river gladdens the city of God. What is this rush of the river? Surely he of whom the Lord speaks through John: whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly. This the Lord Jesus says of the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.

See the magnificence of his majesty. He is so given to the church of God on earth that he nevertheless gladdens the city of God in the heavens. The city of God, that is, the citizens of the heavenly kingdoms, the peoples of the heavenly army, the principalities, powers and dominions, he waters with unspeakable joys in the awareness of eternal blessedness, and more abundantly inebriates with the richness of gladness; he rouses the harmony of heaven to exultation with the torrent of his sanctification. If you suppose that such great things are given through some creature, you leave nothing proper to divine power. If, I say, you think these are given through some creature, you are heading for an insult to the angels and archangels, to whom you think such great things and such are granted through the bounty of a fellow servant.
