SECOND BOOK
THAT NO RATIONAL CREATURE CAN BE INFUSED INTO A KINDRED CREATURE.

We read of the abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit: but Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan. Who, then, could fill him who fills all things, except one who was of the same fullness? Of the apostles the divine word relates: and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with confidence; and a little later: for the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the nations. He is said to fill whole (nations) and is known to remain inexhaustible and full in himself. If the Holy Spirit is created, of what angel or archangel has it ever been read that, received inwardly, he poured himself into any soul? Tell me if you have ever read of any power and might among creatures that fills and possesses many at once and, what is greater, remains undiminished and undivided. It is impossible that a spiritual and rational creature should ever be able to be infused into a nature akin to itself. So too a material thing cannot penetrate a material substance. God alone, in whom the Holy Spirit too is understood, simple, subtle and pure, glides into the thing he made, whether angelic or human, by the power of incorporeal divinity, which alone, penetrating its own work, enters the hidden places of the human heart. But no heavenly creature can so far infuse or fill a man as to be able to know the secrets of human thought. And therefore we read of God alone: you who alone know the hearts of men; and again: for he knows the secrets of the heart. If to know the secrets of man is proper to divinity, how much more is searching the depths of God the mark of the supreme majesty in the person of the Holy Spirit.

To the Author alone is this privilege due, that he can enter the secret place of consciences. A soul can be joined to a soul, or an angel to an angel, but cannot be infused, because kinds of creatures of this sort are capable only of the Holy Spirit, that is, of God alone; because they are the vessels of their potter, they can be filled only by him by whom they were made from nothing and without whom they are felt to be empty. So the substance of the soul, being as it were corporeal matter, cannot at all be infused into another rational creature. For compared with the grossness of the outer man the soul can be called incorporeal, but referred to its Author, to whom his own matter is comprehensible and his handiwork palpable, by whom it can be enclosed and bound within a body and handed over to perpetual fire, as we read: that they may go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels, to this Author it is beyond doubt corporeal, by the Maker's right.

But perhaps you will say: it is plain that the insolent violence of demons too often pours itself into men whom it has received to be tempted. It is not so. For they can enter the hidden recesses of the body, but they cannot reach the inner parts of the soul. It must be understood, then, that the crafty subtlety of the spiritual forces of wickedness disturbs by its assault those regions of the limbs which are at times wearied by too much wine or by the burning of fevers. So hostile temptation knows how to creep into the senses of the soul through malice, but it cannot flow into the recesses of the soul through its nature. And therefore human minds and breasts take in unclean spirits of this kind not by an infusion of natures, but conceive them through depravity of will. It is plain, then, that they cannot penetrate the substances of souls whose consciences they cannot know. And if at times it happens that demons know them, that comes from the betrayal of [the soul's] connivance, not from the power of [their] nature.

Divine power alone, then, which is also in the Holy Spirit, mingles itself with rational creatures, infused into them and poured around them, as in a special way it rested with overflowing grace in that body of the Lord's manhood taken from Mary his mother, as the Son of God himself says of himself: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me. If, then, the Holy Spirit were a thing made, of subject condition, as they say, it would have been as impossible as it was unworthy of God that that creature should fill the soul or body in which the Son of God, that is God, was already present, in which already, as the apostle says, the fullness of the divinity dwelt bodily. If the Holy Spirit is a creature, how can corruption possess incorruption, and a frail condition possess one capable of majesty? If the Holy Spirit is one of the common crowd of things made, how does a creature presume to share one lodging in the Saviour's soul with the Creator, that is with the Son of God, as if on equal terms, a servant with his master, and, as though [the Son] were not sufficient for himself in it, how does the Author's slave come to add to the heap of holiness? It is not so. Rather the heavenly temple recognises the fellowship as its partner; nor is it any wonder if in that illustrious soul of the blessed body the Son and the Holy Spirit are allotted one dwelling, to whom, it is agreed, heaven too is common.
II. WHETHER, ACCORDING TO THE OPINION OF THE UNLEARNED, THE HOLY SPIRIT WAS INCARNATE LIKE THE SON, SINCE HE TOO CAME UPON MARY, OR WHETHER ONLY THE SON WAS BEGOTTEN OF THE VIRGIN.

But it is said: if the Holy Spirit dwelt in the body and soul of the Redeemer, then the Spirit himself too will seem to have taken up incarnation. It is not so. For before the beginnings of the creation [of Christ's humanity] the holy body of Mary is filled by the Holy Spirit, and at the beginnings of that creation the Son of the Virgin is conceived with the Holy Spirit cooperating; but he is infused to be possessed specially by the person of the Son for nine months and to go forth with him into the light, a sharing of which time, within the secret of the virginal womb, the person of the Holy Spirit did not receive. The man, then, whom the Son of God took up at the very beginnings, the Holy Spirit entered not as the one who took him up but as sanctifier; within him, as he acted as Christ's partner, so Christ [acted] as author. For the one is born, the other is infused. Of the Son of the Virgin it can be said personally and specially that he is the soul or flesh of the Son of God, but in no way the soul or flesh of the Holy Spirit. In that in which the Son of God, that is the God of glory, is said to have been crucified, the Holy Spirit can in no way be said to have suffered. There is, then, a diversity of works, not a diversity of substances. For just as we cannot say either that the Father descended in the form of a dove or that the Son spoke in the Father's voice when he said: this is my Son, so we cannot assert that the Holy Spirit was either born of the Virgin or specially lived in the flesh of the Redeemer or was crucified in his passion or restored to the body in the resurrection or raised up to heaven in the ascension. It is fitting, of necessity, that these things be assigned to the work and person of the Son, but it is not fitting that they be ascribed to the Holy Spirit, though the unity of will remains intact.

Amid these things Macedonius asserts that the Holy Spirit is a creature. Let him begin from where it seems good, provided he presumes to accomplish nothing by his own words and does not go beyond the track of the sacred law in a disputation foreign to the holy pages, but brings forward authority throughout [from testimonies], if he can, that may prevail in both number and strength against the faith of the whole world. Without doubt there is need of great allegations and of abundant and very evident proofs for anyone to prove that he is one out of the number of creatures whom all the kingdoms of the earth celebrate together with the Father and the Son as of the same honour and glory, whom the catholic Church, regenerated in him, recognises as her creator. And rightly she does not hesitate to believe him the Author whom she sees to be her restorer.
III. THE OBJECTION OF MACEDONIUS, BY WHICH HE IMPIOUSLY ASSERTS THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT IS A MORE EXCELLENT CREATURE.

'I call him a creature,' you say, 'but more excellent than all creatures.' We have said beforehand that we would arrange our case not by our own persuasions but by catholic oracles. So, as we treat of God, let prophet, apostle and evangelist answer. You call him a creature more excellent than all creatures. Show in which books you have read these words about the Holy Spirit. You will not, I think, show them in the Old, nor in the New. Since, then, you cannot bring them forward, while you do not make good your own case you confirm ours; while you do not prove him a creature, you show, even with us silent, that he is the Creator. Therefore, since this assertion of yours belongs neither to the catholic sense nor at all to Christian teaching, recognise in it the invention of the devil, who, where he sees the house of the soul empty of the Holy Spirit, invades it as the contrary spirit with the dreadful company of sevenfold wickedness. For whoever shuts out the one takes in the other. In him was that more excellent creature you speak of, who, shining forth in heavenly brightness, conscious of the gift but ignorant of the Giver, saw that he had, but did not know that he had received; and therefore the glory which in his blessedness he did not understand, in his pride he lost, saying: I will ascend above the stars of the clouds, I will set my seat above the thrones, and I will be like the Most High. He, then, I think, had no one among creatures higher than himself, saw no one between himself and God in rivalry with whom, spurred by pride, he might rise up; and so, seeing no one standing before him in the order of the heavenly army, he presumed to make himself equal to the very Lord of all things. But if, impatient of a greater, he had found anyone more excellent than himself in the heavenly rank, he would rather have tried to compare or prefer himself to that one.

There are two in the heavenly realm: he who rules and those who are ruled, Creator and creature. No third kind has existed between these, greater than the second and lower than the highest. 'More excellent creature' can perhaps be said of the archangels, though they surpass the rest more in rank than in nature. But even the archangels serve the Holy Spirit, one of whom, as a minister, announced his coming to blessed Mary. But you say: see where the prophet Amos clearly designates the Holy Spirit a creature, saying: behold, I who establish the thunder and create the spirit. First, the bare name 'spirit' can in no way be referred to the person of the sanctifying Spirit unless you add either 'Spirit of God' or 'Holy Spirit' or 'the Spirit breathes where he wills', that is, unless you add the dignity either of his work or of his proper name. Next, if you look at the order of the reading, it has shown this creature, more excellent as you assert, to be very lowly, for it describes it as created after the thunder. Hence it would have been inconsistent that, by your sense, it should place this chief work of God after an irrational and insensible element, or join it with one. It would be unworthy to believe this of the person, I will not say of an angel, but of any just man.

It seems, then, closer and friendlier to reason that after the thunder we should understand the blasts of the winds to be signified, as in that [line] in the psalms: the spirit of the storms, which do his word, or that one: sulphur, the spirit of the storms, or: with a violent spirit shattering the ships of Tarshish. 'Spirit' is understood in various ways when it is not specially designated with its privileges. But leaving these aside, question the truth of the Hebrew translation, and there you will detect the shameful error of your persuasion. For there you will find it said outright: for behold, I who form the mountains and create the wind. See on what bare and empty words against God you have relied. See with what a great argument you have armed yourself against the power of the Majesty. And after this are you not afraid to cling to so weak a twig, you who hang over so dreadful a precipice?
4. MACEDONIUS, ASSERTING A DUALITY, DENIES THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT HAS A PERSON OF HIS OWN.

Next you bring in a duality and say that the Holy Spirit does not have a person of his own, and you do not perceive that you have lost the grace of regeneration, you who strive to give offence to the Regenerator, whom divine truth declares to be united with itself in communion of majesty and power, saying: go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. In the name, it says, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The singularity of the name speaks of unity, but the diversity of the appellations speaks of the Trinity. In name, then, one, but in the distinction of persons not one. What is the prerogative of one name in three, if not the undivided concord of the Godhead? Make a step of rank, if you can, where, as God himself attests, you find nothing beyond one. You hear 'three', so that Sabellian impiety may not mingle and confound the unity; you hear 'one', so that Arian perversity may not divide the Trinity; you hear 'Holy Spirit', so that the expressed property of a distinct name may run Macedonius through. So it is not the work of a creature but the incommunicable work of the Creator that is done where the abolition of sins and immunity is bestowed. Yet in this inseparable embrace of majesty, in the property of person the Father is one, the Son is another, the Holy Spirit another, but in divinity [he is] not another thing; and he certainly, if he were not God, could not have a person of his own beside the Father and the Son. Indeed, when the Word passes into flesh and God puts on the condition of a man, and his tabernacle is made round about him, and he wraps his splendour in the darkness of our frailty and makes darkness his hiding place, there is indeed a twofold substance of God and of man, but yet there is one person. Why? Because, when God, taking the form of a servant, is joined to the servant, the lowliness of the lesser is hidden within the reverence of the greater and, emptied out, is consumed by the light of the higher, and so the humanity does not hold the property of a person, the divinity overshadowing or surpassing it. There, then, can be parity of persons where equality of merits and dignities obtains; and therefore you should know that the Holy Spirit, whom you see holding the proper right of a person, possesses one privilege of majesty with the Father and the Son. But if someone objects and says: if in Christ, God and man alike, we speak of two substances, why should we not by like reasoning believe two persons? It is not so. For whoever makes two persons in Christ introduces the impiety of a quaternity, which the nature of things utterly does not admit. Out of two rational and different substances, especially of God and man, of Creator and creature, one cannot be made; but out of two persons one can be made, as we read that head and body, Christ and the Church, hold one person: for, it says, the two shall be in one flesh. And just as among us men the son of the head of a household beside his father, or a slave beside his master, does not have the standing of a person of his own, so in God and man there is indeed a twin substance, but not a twin person, because a person can consume a person, but a substance cannot consume a substance, since a person is a thing of law, a substance a thing of nature.

At this point it seems necessary to establish by testimonies one person and two substances in Christ, God and man alike. Grant one person of God and man in the Redeemer, the person of whom the apostle says: for if they had known the wisdom of God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. If you ask how the inviolable could suffer and the incomprehensible be crucified, the unity of the person brings it about that what the man endured, God is believed to have endured. Again, when the evangelist records: no one has ascended into heaven except him who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven, how does he here assert that the Son of Man, before the passion or resurrection or the day of ascension, both descended from heaven and remains in the heavens, unless this is resolved in accordance with truth through the unity of the person? So too in another place the person of head and body is joined, when one reads: I was hungry and you gave me to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me to drink. What does the unity of the person do here? The man is fed and God is refreshed; the foot is warmed and the head testifies that it feels the warming. He says, then: they would never have crucified the Lord of glory, and conversely: no one has ascended into heaven except him who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven. See how, for the unity of the person, human things are mingled with divine and divine with human. God is crucified, and the man is said to descend from heaven and to remain in heaven.

This being so, let us examine from the sacred books the distinction of the twofold substance. Blessed Moses says: you shall eat the head with the feet and devour its entrails. Let us believe the humanity in the feet and the majesty in the head. So it comes about that, when by searching faith we come to know these things hidden within the letter, we take the entrails of the lamb, that is, the secrets of the mysteries. For the eagerness to search is understood as the greed of devouring; as in another place the same revealer of mysteries suggests the resolution of the twofold substance, saying: foxes have holes and the birds of the sky nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. That is: deceitful heresies and dark or aerial powers have set their seat in human breasts with deep dominion, but as for me, the hearts of unbelievers, who see me as a man in the flesh, do not believe that God lies hidden within the man. For 'holes' and 'nests' signify not passing and momentary dwellings but ones founded in lasting and secure possession, which multiply the serpentine nourishment of vices. The apostle too, the obscurity of the mystery removed, clearly set out the two substances, saying: our fathers, from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever.

But you say: the apostle in the volume of his works confesses only two persons, as he says to the Corinthians: Paul, called an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God; and to the Galatians: Paul, an apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead; and again: one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him. According to these, you say, no mention is made of the Holy Spirit. To put it briefly, you have forgotten that the apostle, full of the Holy Spirit, preached these things about the Father and the Son to the peoples by his inspiration. So, as he spoke of the working of the Father and the Son, he too was not absent who dictated what was to be spoken, according to that [saying]: and no one says 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit. Whoever, then, is to believe or confess or preach Christ, you see, must first have the Holy Spirit in himself. Let it not burden your faith, then, that at times mention is made of the Father and the Son without mention of the Holy Spirit. For often, the name of the Father being suppressed, the working of the Son and the Holy Spirit is preached. Holy Ananias says to Paul: brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, sent me, so that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Here plainly is a conjunction of two persons. See, Paul is rebuked by Christ in being blinded, is filled by the Holy Spirit in being enlightened, and no mention of the Father is inserted here.

Again, when Paul questioned certain of the disciples: into what were you baptized? — those who, it was established, had been baptized with the baptism of John after the Lord's ascension, after the baptism of the Trinity had been preached, when even that mystery with which John had been accustomed to baptize, that is, into him who is to come, was shown to have been omitted in their baptism, the apostle Paul saying to them: John indeed baptized, but into him who is to come, which is to say: you were not baptized so — when Paul asked them: did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? — who certainly ought to have been confessed by those duly baptized, after the Saviour's baptism, through the laying on of hands — they answered: we have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit. Having heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. Notice that, when they are baptized in the name of Jesus, they afterwards receive the Holy Spirit and prophetic power from the invocation of the Paraclete. Truly he is God who after the gift of God adds increase to fullness.

See, two persons being signified in the baptism, the Father is not read to have been invoked; yet, as one must believe, he works with the Son and the Holy Spirit in unity of power and Godhead, and the sacred reading was silent about his presence, but did not deny it. When the Holy Spirit had come upon them, then they spoke in tongues and prophesied. See how great the power of the Holy Spirit is. In baptism the remission of sins is granted; at the coming of the Holy Spirit the gifts of virtues are conferred, and miracles of signs are performed by the confirmed. But those estranged from the truth are wont to raise false charges even about syllables. For since we know it said outright of the Trinity: for from him and through him and in him are all things, they assert that 'from him' is more than 'through him', and again that this preposition, that is 'through', is of greater prerogative than 'in him'. But if they think 'in him' is said of the Holy Spirit with a diminution of power, let them hear the magnificence of this preposition and accept it, since even by their own assertion it is to be understood of the Holy Spirit. In him, it says, we live and move and are. And rightly do we live and move and are in him in whom we have been restored and regenerated. But we know that 'through him' too is to be referred to the Holy Spirit, as you have: to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge; again to the Hebrews: who through the Holy Spirit offered himself spotless to God; and again: the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. For although we understand 'from him' of the Father, we likewise quite often find it said 'from the Holy Spirit', as we have in the Gospel of John: what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit; and at the end of the passage: so is everyone, it says, who is born of the Spirit.

So, then, it does not prejudice the Holy Spirit when, his name being suppressed, the works of the Father and the Son are recalled, just as the Father and the Son are not denied when a work or power of the Holy Spirit specifically is asserted, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now; and as is also contained in the Gospel concerning the single person of the Holy Spirit: unless someone has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. Will the Father and the Son be believed to have been absent from so great and so divine a gift in this place, because they are not named at all? It is not so. For without doubt they are joined in the mysteries and benefits with the Holy Spirit, with whom they have one substance, and, if not by mention, yet by unity of grace and of work they are present.
V. The objection that the saying we read, 'unless someone has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit', testifies that water and the Holy Spirit alike are a creature.

But you say: the Holy Spirit is a creature to such a degree that he seems to be joined to the element of water, which is placed here in first position and order, according to the Gospel saying recalled above: unless someone has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. It is plain that whoever says this is ignorant not only of the divine power in the Holy Spirit but of the very meaning of baptism. Now the apostle says: but if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with Christ. And if you ask how we can either die or rise with Christ, take note. All of us who are plunged into the sacred font imitate the death and burial of the Redeemer, as the same apostle says: or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ have been baptized into his death? For we have been buried with Christ through baptism into death. For just as he was laid in the tomb by a three-day death, so we too, set down within the water, that is, within the bosom of a kindred creature, by a threefold immersion, are buried as we go down and are raised as we come up. Through the water, then, the imitation of burial is performed; through the Holy Spirit the reality of life and the hope of eternal salvation are conferred. In short, let the invocation of the Holy Spirit be removed, and let us see whether the pouring of that water alone can be of any benefit. It is a creature, therefore, that imitates the office of burying; it is God who grants the benefit of being reborn. Him, then, whom you perceive as the parent of restoration, know to be also the author of resurrection. Of him the prophet foretells, speaking thus to the Father: send forth your Spirit and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth. What is the difference between the working of the water and that of the Holy Spirit? Through the water we are seen to be led down into the tomb; through the Holy Spirit we are proved to be made ready for the kingdom.
VI. Where it is asked whether the designation 'Holy Spirit' is to be thought a surname or a name.

But amid these things you think it must be asked whether the designation 'Holy Spirit', who must also be called God, is a name or perhaps a surname. But recognize that what we are accustomed among men to add to a name does not befit the majesty of God, in whose name whatever there is is in no way added on, but without doubt is eternal by nature. Even the teaching of grammar calls some nouns common, that is, appellative, and names others special, that is, proper. Let us see whether we can find anything similar in our own [matters] here. Grant in God a special or proper name, that is, Father and Son and Holy Spirit. These are proper to such a degree that the Son cannot be called Father, nor is the Father readily read of as Holy Spirit. Again, grant a proper [name]: unbegotten, begotten, proceeding from both. Again, grant a general and common name: majesty, immensity, fullness, one, the only God. But when you hear 'one', number does not begin here; rather, infinite perfection is gathered together. What is 'one' but an incommunicable name, which admits neither a later nor an earlier? What is 'one' but a simple, uncompounded and undivided substance? What is 'one' but unchangeable and equal and always the same, who can never be different from himself? And so the common designation speaks the unity, the proper one the Trinity. When, therefore, you have said Father, Son, Holy Spirit, you have set out specifically the persons of each; when you have said one God, you have shown the common substance of the Trinity, the common glory. Here, then, ignorance has drawn over itself the night of error, when, suppressing the word of majesty, it reckons the Holy Spirit only in that name which, as we have said, is proper to him, rather than in what he has in common with the Father and the Son.
VII. That the Holy Spirit specifically fills the prophets, and is likewise to be believed and called God, is proved by clear testimonies.

Since the Holy Spirit is reported to have spoken specifically through Moses and David and Isaiah or other prophets, divine [Scripture] declares that God spoke, as occurs frequently in the volume of the Pentateuch: the Lord spoke, it says, to Moses, saying. Let us inquire more carefully whether the Holy Spirit specifically speaks in the prophets. We have, as we said before, in the Acts of the Apostles, when Paul is refuting the Jews: well, he says, did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah to our fathers: hearing you will hear and not understand; [and] in the same reading: men, brothers, the scripture must be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David. And in the epistle of Peter we read: for prophecy was never brought by human will, but the holy men of God spoke by the Holy Spirit. Let us acknowledge that prophetic grace plainly belongs to the power of the Holy Spirit. And concerning a psalm of David we read thus to the Hebrews: therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: today, if you hear his voice, and so on. Here too it testifies most plainly that the Holy Spirit spoke through David.

Let us see, however, whether he through whom all prophecy is recorded as inspired is God. Luke asserts that it is the Lord God who spoke through the prophets, saying thus: blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and brought about the redemption of his people; and he adds: as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, who are from of old. Absolutely is the Holy Spirit, who had inspired the prophets, proclaimed by the Gospel oracle to be the Lord and God of Israel. And in what follows, Simeon, full of the Holy Spirit: he had received, it says, an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ. When he had seen him and taken him into his arms in an embrace, he blessed God, that is, the one from whom he was seen to have received the answer; he blessed God and said: now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace. See, he absolutely calls Lord and God the Holy Spirit, by whose word and answer he had received [the promise] that he would see Christ. You see that it is to be understood specifically of the Holy Spirit when it is said in the prophets: the God of gods, the Lord, has spoken; and: I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me. Here know that this name, that is, Lord God, is to be referred to the person of the Holy Spirit, who spoke in David, or at any rate recognize in the one God the will of the three, the power of the three, the substance of the three, since, when you have said Father, the person of one is understood; when you have said God, the whole Trinity is designated.

We also learn in the Acts of the Apostles that he who had foretold the sufferings of Christ through the prophets is undoubtedly God. For it says thus: but God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has thus fulfilled [it] — his Christ, that is, the one imbued with the gift of grace of his anointing; and again: what God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old. As for its saying 'what God spoke through the mouth of his holy ones', [it says] 'his holy ones' because sanctification belongs properly to the Holy Spirit. We read in Isaiah: do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord? Who is this Lord who says through Isaiah that he fills heaven and earth, if not the Holy Spirit, who filled Isaiah himself with prophetic power and the spirit of truth? Just as, then, with the prophetic dispensation, so too the will of the Trinity assigns the grace of the second birth above all to the Holy Spirit, as it says in John: what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit. And in another place the power of renewing man is written as lying with the Holy Spirit: but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now; and, as was said above: unless someone has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit; and to Titus: he saved us, it says, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. Let us see who this is whose sons we are made through the grace of adoption: he gave them, it says, power to become sons of God; and again: who were born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh, but of God.

You see most plainly that this Holy Spirit, in whom we are reborn, is God, by whose fatherhood we are endowed. He himself assigns this more clearly than light in another place: I will be, he says, a father to them, and they will be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord almighty. Rightly almighty, who blots out the bond of sin, who loosens the chains of consciences, and strips the man who believes in him of the foulness of corrupted nature, and adorns him with the garment of innocence, the beauty of righteousness, the robe of immortality, and with loving fatherhood transfers his sons into the angelic state. Let no one think that the Holy Spirit is to be classed with creatures. He who can bestow eternal freedom is outside the condition of servitude. For you did not receive, says the apostle, the spirit of servitude again in fear, but you received the spirit of adoption of sons; and the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God. Without doubt he is God who, through the remission of sins, makes sons of God.

It is agreed that the whole creation, even of angels and archangels, was liable to sin; yet the fall of the transgressors made firm their obedience, care and love toward God. It became a confirmation of humility, subjection and steadfastness, and an acknowledgement of frailty. The Holy Spirit, unless he were free above all, could not make free men out of slaves. For if he were a creature, however much God conferred on him the grace of holiness, the consciousness of a debtor would still have remained. And therefore it says: no one can forgive sins but God alone. Whoever he is, let him choose which he wants: either let him confess that the Holy Spirit, who forgives sins, is God in every respect, or, if he does not believe that pardon of sins can be granted through him, he has emptied out for himself the benefit of regeneration and the sacrament of baptism. It belongs, then, to God alone to release what is bound, to restore what is corrupted, to cleanse what is stained. And therefore, conscious of our weakness and of his majesty, we cry out to him with groaning: against you alone have I sinned; that is, you who alone are not held by the law of sin, who alone are a stranger to it not in act but by nature, and therefore alone can release debtors, you who alone are free from debts, who have not borrowed from elsewhere what you have, but are full of your own. For no one gave to you first, nor are you watered by powers drawn from elsewhere, nor has any transfusion been made into you from some other, but you yourself are the fountain of your own river and your own glory. Yours is a nature which, as it knows no beginning, so has received nothing from anyone before it.
VIII. Where the temple of God is shown to be the temple of the Holy Spirit.

The sacred oracles define the indweller of the human heart as properly the Holy Spirit: the Father, it says, will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you for ever; and to the Corinthians: he will give life also to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you. And therefore we rightly understand as written of the Holy Spirit: the kingdom of God is within you. They indeed are the kingdom of God who deserve to prepare themselves for him as a temple, a temple of God, that is, not of a creature. Hear through the apostle the voice of our indweller: you are, he says, the temple of the living God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you; and in another place: as God says: I will dwell in them and walk among them and I will be their God. See, he who dwells in the temple of the human heart declares himself to be God. Ananias, among those who, honouring God, sold their possessions acquired by their just labours and laid [the proceeds] at the feet of the apostles, is known to have promised a vow to God, and is charged with having lied to the Holy Spirit, as the apostle Peter says: Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit? And following on he added: you have not lied to men, but to God. What is this? Does he sin against the Creator, and does scripture so lessen his sin as to establish, according to the sense of impiety, that he is guilty toward a creature, and assign him as debtor to a lesser being for an insult to a greater? It is not so. He is plainly endowed with divine power to whom the offence of sacrilege is referred, of whom it says in another place: but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not have forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the one to come. Since, then, he tempted God by his transgression, he is said to have deceived the Holy Spirit. Therefore recognize one cause, one glory, one reverence of the Holy Spirit and of God. And therefore, most evidently concerning the Holy Spirit, he concluded in the following words: you have not, he says, lied to men, but to God.

While Peter was speaking to Cornelius, the faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on the gentiles too. You see that the Holy Spirit conferred grace not from what belonged to another, but from his own. If you ask who this is who gave the grace, he taught it next, saying: if, then, God gave them the same grace. This giver of grace he declared above to be the Holy Spirit, here specifically God. There by the proper name, here by the common name, the repeated confession is proved. And when he says: and the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out on the gentiles, he who is the author of grace is God by nature. It belongs to God alone to bestow the gifts of grace from his own, so that the apostle too seems to have said of him: I laboured more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me. Rightly is he declared God who is the dispenser of grace and of human salvation. And Peter adds: who was I, that I could hinder God? That God, certainly, who poured himself out on the gentiles and on Cornelius with the rush of overflowing grace.
IX. Where, against the Novatians, God gave the gentiles repentance unto life; and that this God is the Holy Spirit is shown by the very order of the reading.

Notice how, in the person of the Holy Spirit, who suddenly filled Cornelius and his companions, the name of God is celebrated with manifold attestation: when they heard these things, it says, they fell silent and glorified God, saying: so God has given repentance unto life to the gentiles too. In this place it must be noted against the Novatians that he is said to give repentance, which he certainly bestows in no other way than through the ministry of his servants. When, then, it says: who was I, that I could hinder God, and again: so God has given repentance unto life to the gentiles, what interpretation is to be awaited in matters so plain, when the confession of the divine name, repeated so many times at the coming of the Holy Spirit, would not satisfy either the ignorant or the unbelieving?
X. Where, in First Corinthians, the Holy Spirit is declared to be God by the distributions of powers.

Take from Corinthians what alone could suffice to assert the divinity of the Holy Spirit. He says in the epistle to the Hebrews: God bearing witness with signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will. Let us ask the apostle himself whether this distributor of the gifts of grace is one of the creatures. We have in First Corinthians: I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says anathema to Jesus, and no one can say Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit. Notice how he here most absolutely designated the Spirit of God as the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Holy Spirit, whom in the preceding sentence he presented as the Spirit of God speaking, look at what follows, how manifestly it testifies that he is God and Lord: there are divisions, it says, of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God. As if the blessed apostle had been consulted about the divinity of the Holy Spirit, he plainly adds of the one of whom he had said: the same Spirit, the words: the same God, who works all things in all. He could not work all things if he were one among all. Here recognize the Holy Spirit, both under his own name and under Lord and God, either evidently expressed or at any rate associated with the Trinity. But here the divine word is understood to have designated the Holy Spirit rather in the divisions of the gifts, since we learned above that the grace of the distributions belongs to the Holy Spirit by a special dispensation. And what he said: the same Lord, but the same God, he shows in the following passage is to be referred to the Holy Spirit, saying: to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the grace of healings in the one Spirit, to another the working of powers, to another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of speech. But all these things the one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each as he wills. He is subject to no one, but is the heavenly Lord, who bestows heavenly gifts by his own will and by the right of his own power.
XI. It is to be noted that, just as he speaks of one God, so he speaks of one Holy Spirit, which could in no way be said of a common creature, nor that it divides to each as it wills.

You see that, just as there is one Father and one Son, so too there is one Holy Spirit, as he assigns next: for in one Spirit we have been given to drink. If he were of the common crowd or multitude of creation, he could not be called one at all. And since you have here: to another, it says, faith is given in the same Spirit, the same apostle declared to the Corinthians who it is that bestows this faith, saying: and to each as God has divided the measure of faith. You see that he declares without doubt that this divider of faith is God. Although in so manifold a bounty of such great gifts the very magnificence of the work by itself speaks the power of its author, yet he concluded about him thus: but all these things the one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each as he wills; as also in another place: the Spirit breathes where he wills; and again: and by distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will. Here, then, is not the ministry of subject servitude, but the free decision of free power, and in the distributions of heavenly goods there is the inexhaustible kindness of supreme bounty. As to his saying: and by distributions of the Holy Spirit, whether this distributor, that is, divider, is God, he taught to the Corinthians, saying: and there are divisions of operations, but the same God. We read in the Acts of the Apostles: take heed, it says, to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has set you as bishops to rule the church of God. This one, who set bishops in the church, the vessel of election declares to the Corinthians to be God, saying thus: and some God has set in the church. What God, if not the Holy Spirit, whose personal office the distribution of graces shows, as follows in the continuous passage: God has set, it says, in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then graces of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues. Some, it says, God has set in the church. That here he said God of the Holy Spirit is made manifest by the very dispensation of sanctifications and powers, which belongs to the Holy Spirit. For he enriches the mouths of the prophets, dispenses the remedies of healings, multiplies the adornments of the gifts of grace; and as he flowed into the apostles, the miracles of signs and the various kinds of tongues proclaimed him to be the God of the universe.
XII. Where he says that those who have been made the temple of the Holy Spirit ought so to advance that they may be worthy to carry God in the body.

And so the apostle says to the Corinthians: do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit? That the temple of the Holy Spirit is the temple of God, the preceding parts of the same epistle evidently suggest, when they say: or do you not know that you are the temple of God and the Holy Spirit dwells in you? And the Holy Spirit, he says, dwells in you. Who would doubt that they are the temple of that God whose dwelling-place they are shown to be? And when he had said: do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, he concluded the passage with this clear truth: glorify, he says, and carry God in your body. Therefore he who zealously prepares in his heart a temple of purity for the Holy Spirit carries God in the body through chastity and the mortification of the flesh; he must carry bodily the one by whom we are spiritually possessed. Wherefore him whom you see worthy of a temple, know that he is to be adored with divine honours, celebrated with vows, and worshipped with sacrifices. So the teacher of the Gentiles speaks to the universal church: do you not know that you are the temple of God and the Holy Spirit dwells in you? This is possible for no creature, but it is the mark of the divine majesty, that he should fill peoples one by one, in each individual, and yet remain in the immensity of his fullness. It is, I say, the singular and proper attribute of the divine nature to be present in all places, to enter into all things, to contain all things. It is, I say, peculiar to God to strip the sons of perdition of what is owed to [their] nature, to renew [them] with cleansed consciences, to make [them] sons of God and to raise [them] up into the glory of the heavenly kingdom.
